meta.title: Who really said "Don't talk of peace and love when you have a dead animal on your plate"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Socrates. He wrote nothing, so everything attributed to him is second-hand — chiefly Plato and Xenophon, plus Aristophanes, Aristotle, and later compilers such as Diogenes Laërtius. The line appears in none of the surviving Socratic literature. The real Socratic passage on meat is stranger and better.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Don't talk of peace and love when you have a dead animal on your plate'?
meta.ogDescription: A modern slogan in a toga. Socrates left no writings, and the line is absent from the surviving Socratic literature — but Plato's Socrates really does argue that the appetite for meat is what drags a city into war.

answer.label: Nobody in antiquity — origin unlocated
answer.authorDates: Anonymous · origin unlocated; circulates as a captioned slogan
answer.sourceLine: There is no ancient source for this. Socrates wrote nothing at all, so everything attributed to him is second-hand — chiefly Plato and Xenophon, plus Aristophanes’ hostile comedy, Aristotle, and later compilers such as Diogenes Laërtius. The sentence appears in none of the surviving Socratic literature, and no direct injunction against eating meat is attributed to him — though Plato’s Socrates does trace war back to the appetite for meat (see below). The wording is modern English advocacy prose; it circulates as a caption, never with a citation.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Origin unlocated — first known circulation is modern, as a captioned slogan
None — absent from the surviving Socratic literature

source.excerpt: True, I replied, I had forgotten; of course they must have a relish—salt, and olives, and cheese, and they will boil roots and herbs such as country people prepare; for a dessert we shall give them figs, and peas, and beans; and they will roast myrtle-berries and acorns at the fire, drinking in moderation. And with such a diet they may be expected to live in peace and health to a good old age… Then a slice of our neighbours’ land will be wanted by us for pasture and tillage, and they will want a slice of ours… And so we shall go to war, Glaucon. Shall we not?
trail: Start with the fact that makes this checkable: Socrates left no writings. There is no lost notebook to appeal to; everything attributed to him is second-hand, and the accounts do not always agree — the ‘Socratic problem’. The fullest come from his pupils Plato and Xenophon, with Aristophanes’ hostile comedy staged in his lifetime and Aristotle writing after his death; later compilers such as Diogenes Laërtius gather anecdotes centuries on. Across that surviving literature the sentence simply does not appear the sources for Socrates ↗.

The sentence is also modern in build. ‘Don’t talk of peace and love’ is the cadence of a twentieth-century protest placard, not of a Greek dialogue, and no version of it exists in Greek. Nobody who circulates it offers a dialogue, a section number, or a translator.

The nearest genuine passage runs the argument the other way round, and is worth having. In Republic Book II, Socrates builds his ‘true and healthy’ city on olives, cheese, figs, roots and beans. Glaucon complains that this is a city fit for pigs and demands proper food; Socrates obliges with a ‘State at fever-heat’ that needs swineherds, hunters and ‘animals of many other kinds, if people eat them’ — and then needs its neighbours’ land for pasture. ‘And so we shall go to war, Glaucon’ Republic, Jowett translation ↗.
source.excerptNote: This is not the quote. It is the real thing standing behind it: Plato’s Socrates describing a meatless city, being told it is a city of pigs, adding meat — and arriving four steps later at war. The slogan asserts a link between the plate and peace by scolding. Socrates argues it, and the argument is his own.

source.rightsNote: We cannot state a rights status, so we do not guess one. The slogan is modern and anonymous: somebody wrote it, probably within living memory, and an unidentified author is not the same thing as a free one. Treat it as text of unknown ownership and do not build a product on it. The material we quote here is clear — Benjamin Jowett’s Victorian translation (Jowett died 1893) is long out of copyright, and Plato needs no permission. This is not legal advice.

author.name: Socrates
author.heading: Why it gets pinned on Socrates
author.metaLine: c. 470–399 BC · Athenian philosopher who wrote nothing
author.bio: Socrates is the ideal host for an invented quotation, because he published nothing and therefore cannot be checked against himself. He was also famously austere — barefoot, indifferent to comfort, contemptuous of appetite — which makes a line about renouncing meat sound plausible in his voice. The austerity is real; the vegetarianism is imported. The ancient philosopher who genuinely campaigned against eating animals was Pythagoras, a century earlier, and the great surviving polemic is Plutarch’s, five centuries later. Socrates simply is not part of that tradition.

misattribution.heading: The attribution problem
misattribution.intro: This one is used in earnest, by people arguing for something they believe. That is exactly why the citation matters: a fabricated authority is the weakest brick you can put in a real argument, and the genuine ancient material is stronger anyway.

items.who: Modern English, no Greek behind it
items.why: Genuine translated quotations have a Greek text somewhere upstream and a translator’s name attached. This has neither — it exists only in English, and only as a caption. The variants drift freely too: ‘love and peace,’ ‘dead animals in your plate.’

Ancient Greek vegetarianism is a Pythagorean movement, and its surviving masterpiece is Plutarch’s essay On the Eating of Flesh. If you want an ancient voice on your side, quote Plutarch — he actually wrote it down the essay ↗.

items.scope: What Socrates really said about meat
items.why: He describes a healthy city living on figs, olives, cheese and beans, is mocked for it, adds meat to please his critic — and watches the city expand, covet its neighbours’ pasture and go to war. The slogan scolds; the passage argues Republic II ↗.

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: It works as a slogan because it catches someone mid-sentence. You are talking about peace; it points at your dinner and says you have already lost the argument. That is a placard’s job, and it does it well — which is also why it needs a 2,400-year-old signature to feel like more than a jab.
The irony is that borrowing Socrates weakens it. He is the philosopher who refused to assert things he could not defend, and the line asks you to accept an accusation on his authority alone.
context.detailsSummary: The surviving record of Socrates, and why the line isn’t in it
detailsBody: Socrates wrote nothing. Not a dialogue, not a letter, not a fragment.
Plato: the dialogues, our fullest portrait, and freely philosophical rather than stenographic.
Xenophon: the Memorabilia and related works, a plainer and more domestic Socrates.
Aristophanes: the Clouds, a hostile comedy staged in his lifetime.
Aristotle: born after Socrates died, but close to the circle and reporting on him.
Later compilers such as Diogenes Laërtius gather anecdotes centuries on, and others — Aeschines, Antisthenes, Cebes, Phaedo — wrote about him too.
The accounts are second-hand and do not always agree — the ‘Socratic problem’. But across all of it, this sentence never appears.
context.pull: He wrote nothing. Everything we have of him is second-hand — and this line is in none of it.
